source_refs.note: Topic 12.2.2 with Figure 12.2 and the Did You Know box, printed pages 275-276.

blocks.text: The ammonia molecule is pyramidal because of the lone pair on nitrogen. When the nitrogen atom uses this lone pair to form ammonium, the ion adopts a tetrahedral shape in which all four bonds are of equal length and strength (Figure 12.2). The ammonium ion is formed by an acid-base reaction: the lone pair accepts a proton from an acid. IUPAC also recommends the names azane for ammonia and azanium for ammonium, from azote, a Greek-derived name for nitrogen meaning 'no life', used in naming derivatives such as sodium azide, NaN3.

blocks.alt: Left: ammonia, NH3, drawn in 3D style with one bond as a wedge (towards you) and one as dashes (away); a lone pair sits on top of the nitrogen, making the molecule pyramidal. An arrow labelled + H+ shows the lone pair bonding to a proton. Right: ammonium, NH4+, with four hydrogens round the nitrogen in a tetrahedral shape and four equal N-H bonds.
blocks.caption: Pyramidal ammonia and tetrahedral ammonium (original diagram after Figure 12.2).

blocks.prompt: Explain how the ammonium ion is formed and why its shape differs from that of ammonia (MCQ III).
blocks.explanation: Ammonia's nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, which repel into a pyramid. When an acid supplies a proton, the lone pair bonds to it, giving nitrogen four identical bonding pairs with no lone pair; four equal pairs spread into a regular tetrahedron, so NH4+ is tetrahedral.

items: NH3 pyramidal (lone pair); the lone pair takes H+ to give NH4+, tetrahedral with four equal N-H bonds; IUPAC names azane and azanium.
